t: Minimum Total Cost to Make Arrays Unequal — Greedy on Conflict Set
o: Only indices where nums1[i] == nums2[i] are problematic; call them the conflict set S. Swaps involving only indices outside S waste money, so ideally we permute values within S so no position matches. Within S, think of it as rearranging multiset values; a value v occurring c_v times in S can be fixed internally iff 2·max(c_v) <= |S| (pair up conflicting duplicates with other values). Then the cost is simply sum of indices in S. If one value dominates (2·max > |S|), we must import one outside index j whose nums2[j] differs from the dominant value, adding j to the cost — pick the smallest such j. Example 3 fails because value 2 occupies all conflict slots with no relief possible.
k: Conflict set S = {i : nums1[i]==nums2[i]}; everything else already satisfies the constraint.
If 2·max frequency <= |S|, internal rearrangement suffices: cost = Σ S.
Otherwise one extra index j ∉ S with nums2[j] != dominant value is needed: cost = Σ S + min such j; if none exists, return -1.

a.n: Approach 1: Frequency Analysis of the Conflict Set
a.i: Collect S and count value frequencies of nums1 restricted to S. Balanced case: a derangement-like arrangement exists (standard pairing argument), cost = sum(S). Dominant case: each internal swap fixes at most two copies of the majority value v, so we need ⌈extra⌉ external swaps; one external index j suffices only if bringing nums1[j]'s partner arrangement works — the known correct criterion is: pick the smallest j ∉ S with nums2[j] != v (swapping v out to j keeps nums1[j]=v != nums2[j] and injects a fresh value into S). If no such j exists, impossible (-1).
s: Build S and freq counts of nums1[i] for i in S; if S empty return 0.
Find dominant value v with max frequency; if 2·freq[v] <= |S|, return sum(S).
Else scan j from 0 upward for j ∉ S with nums2[j] != v; return sum(S)+j if found, else -1.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def minimumTotalCost(self, nums1, nums2):
        from collections import Counter
        n=len(nums1)
        S=[i for i in range(n) if nums1[i]==nums2[i]]
        if not S: return 0
        cnt=Counter(nums1[i] for i in S)
        v,mx=cnt.most_common(1)[0]
        base=sum(S)
        if 2*mx<=len(S): return base
        for j in range(n):
            if j not in set(S) and nums2[j]!=v:
                return base+j
        return -1

a.t: O(n) — a few linear scans with hash-map updates.
a.sp: O(n) — conflict flags and frequency map.

w: Why is one external index enough in the dominant case? Because each swap can place at most two copies of v into non-conflicting spots, and the imported index supplies the 'slack' capacity of 1, turning 2·mx <= m+1 into satisfiability. Pitfall: forgetting that the external j must avoid S and must have nums2[j] != v (otherwise the swap recreates a conflict at j). Verify impossibility carefully — it happens exactly when every non-conflict index holds value v in nums2. Follow-up: what if swap costs were arbitrary weights — then it becomes a matching/flow problem.
